papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: SOM Directions are Better than One: Multi-Directional Refusal Suppression in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is refusal behavior in language models better represented by a single linear direction or by a low-dimensional manifold of multiple directions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a multi-directional approach using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to model refusal as a manifold, showing that ablating multiple directions is more effective for refusal suppression than ablating a single direction.
papers.conclusion: Modeling refusal as a manifold spanned by multiple, closely related directions provides a more faithful and effective view of safety-related behaviors in LLMs than the single-direction perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating multiple refusal directions identified by SOMs (MD) significantly outperforms the single-direction baseline (SD) and other jailbreak algorithms (GCG, SAA) in terms of Attack Success Rate (ASR).
Ablating multiple directions compresses the variance of harmful prompt representations and shifts them closer to harmless representations in the model's activation space.
The multiple directions extracted by SOMs are closely related (non-orthogonal), suggesting refusal is encoded as a manifold rather than a set of orthogonal components.
The method is effective even against a model with a defense mechanism (Mistral-7B-RR).
The effectiveness of refusal suppression generally increases with the number of ablated directions (k).
papers.limitation:
The Bayesian Optimization search for the best combination of directions can require a high number of trials as the search space grows, impacting scalability and speed.
The method computes directions at a single layer and applies ablation uniformly across all layers, potentially missing layer-specific variations in refusal encoding.
future_direction: Explore more efficient or structured search strategies, gradient-based optimization, or pruning algorithms to improve the scalability of the direction search.
Investigate layer-specific directions and ablation strategies to better capture refusal encoding across different layers.
Investigate the effectiveness of training separate SOMs for harmless prompts instead of using a single centroid.
papers.abstract: Refusal refers to the functional behavior enabling safety-aligned language models to reject harmful or unethical prompts. Following the growing scientific interest in mechanistic interpretability, recent work encoded refusal behavior as a single direction in the model's latent space; e.g., computed as the difference between the centroids of harmful and harmless prompt representations. However, emerging evidence suggests that concepts in LLMs often appear to be encoded as a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional latent space. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method leveraging Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to extract multiple refusal directions. To this end, we first prove that SOMs generalize the prior work's difference-in-means technique. We then train SOMs on harmful prompt representations to identify multiple neurons. By subtracting the centroid of harmless representations from each neuron, we derive a set of multiple directions expressing the refusal concept. We validate our method on an extensive experimental setup, demonstrating that ablating multiple directions from models' internals outperforms not only the single-direction baseline but also specialized jailbreak algorithms, leading to an effective suppression of refusal. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the mechanistic implications of our approach.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms and causal features that govern refusal behavior in large language models when presented with harmful prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline combining sparse autoencoders and factorization machines to isolate causal features for LLM refusal, revealing redundant 'hydra' features that activate when others are suppressed.
papers.conclusion: Presents a pipeline for isolating causal refusal features using SAEs and factorization machines, revealing feature redundancy and interactions, laying groundwork for feature-level steering of refusal behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating specific SAE features can jailbreak models, flipping refusal to compliance on harmful prompts.
Redundant features exist that remain dormant until other features are ablated, demonstrating a hydra effect in refusal mechanisms.
Factorization machines capture non-linear feature interactions better than linear probes for identifying jailbreak-critical features.
Jailbreak-critical features can be mapped to harm categories in an unsafe taxonomy, though with limited human alignment.
The refusal mechanism involves non-linear interactions among features, as shown by the superior performance of factorization machines over linear probes.
papers.limitation:
Generality limited to two model sizes; larger models untested.
SAE stability issues due to sensitivity to training data and initialization.
High computational cost for searching and evaluating features across benchmarks.
future_direction: Characterize the safety benefits and risks of redundancy
Evaluate how varied jailbreak strategies perturb the activation space
Analyze prompts that resist jailbreak to uncover protective circuits
papers.abstract: Refusal on harmful prompts is a key safety behaviour in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), yet the internal causes of this behaviour remain poorly understood. We study two public instruction-tuned models, Gemma-2-2B-IT and LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT, using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual-stream activations. Given a harmful prompt, we search the SAE latent space for feature sets whose ablation flips the model from refusal to compliance, demonstrating causal influence and creating a jailbreak. Our search proceeds in three stages: (1) Refusal Direction: find a refusal-mediating direction and collect SAE features near that direction; (2) Greedy Filtering: prune to a minimal set; and (3) Interaction Discovery: fit a factorization machine (FM) that captures nonlinear interactions among the remaining active features and the minimal set. This pipeline yields a broad set of jailbreak-critical features, offering insight into the mechanistic basis of refusal. Moreover, we find evidence of redundant features that remain dormant unless earlier features are suppressed. Our findings highlight the potential for fine-grained auditing and targeted intervention in safety behaviours by manipulating the interpretable latent space.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
Linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses (style).
Sparse autoencoders uncover a structured internal representation: a small reusable core of shared refusal latents supplemented by a long tail of style- and domain-specific latents.
Linear interventions collapse over this structure, flattening mechanistic differences into uniform behavioral control.
papers.limitation:
The techniques could be misused to suppress refusal behavior and facilitate the generation of harmful content.
Linear steering collapses a rich internal refusal structure into a coarse behavioral knob, underscoring that such interventions are not suitable as principled safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Prior work argues that refusal in large language models is mediated by a single activation-space direction, enabling effective steering and ablation. We show that this account is incomplete. Across eleven categories of refusal and non-compliance, including safety, incomplete or unsupported requests, anthropomorphization, and over-refusal, we find that these refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet despite this diversity, linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal to over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob. The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: Hallucinate Less by Thinking More: Aspect-Based Causal Abstention for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enable early abstention in Large Language Models by analyzing the internal diversity of their parametric knowledge through causal inference to prevent unreliable responses?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a framework that enables early abstention in LLMs by modeling knowledge heterogeneity through aspect-conditioned causal inference, improving abstention reliability and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: ABCA provides a causally principled framework for early abstention by probing diverse knowledge aspects, effectively reducing hallucinations and offering interpretable abstention decisions.
papers.key_findings:
ABCA achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple abstention benchmarks, outperforming existing post-hoc methods.
The framework distinguishes between knowledge conflict (Type-1) and knowledge insufficiency (Type-2) abstention, providing interpretable decisions.
ABCA improves answering accuracy on answerable questions while maintaining high abstention accuracy on unanswerable ones.
The dual-agent aspect discovery mechanism effectively identifies causally valid conditioning variables and aspects.
Case studies reveal limitations such as invalid aspect conditioning leading to incorrect abstention and aggregation on spurious facts despite consensus.
papers.limitation:
Invalid aspect conditioning (e.g., using a non-meaningful dimension like 'Number of') can lead to incorrect abstention decisions.
Strong agreement across discovered aspects may still lead to incorrect answers if the aspects overlook disambiguating information in the query.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce fluent but factually incorrect responses, a phenomenon known as hallucination. Abstention, where the model chooses not to answer and instead outputs phrases such as "I don't know", is a common safeguard. However, existing abstention methods typically rely on post-generation signals, such as generation variations or feedback, which limits their ability to prevent unreliable responses in advance. In this paper, we introduce Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a new framework that enables early abstention by analysing the internal diversity of LLM knowledge through causal inference. This diversity reflects the multifaceted nature of parametric knowledge acquired from various sources, representing diverse aspects such as disciplines, legal contexts, or temporal frames. ABCA estimates causal effects conditioned on these aspects to assess the reliability of knowledge relevant to a given query. Based on these estimates, we enable two types of abstention: Type-1, where aspect effects are inconsistent (knowledge conflict), and Type-2, where aspect effects consistently support abstention (knowledge insufficiency). Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ABCA improves abstention reliability, achieves state-of-the-art performance, and enhances the interpretability of abstention decisions.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Latent Adversarial Training Improves the Representation of Refusal
papers.research_question: How does Latent Adversarial Training (LAT) affect the underlying representation of refusal behavior in language models compared to supervised safety fine-tuning (SSFT) and embedding space adversarial training (AT)?
papers.core_contribution: LAT reorganizes refusal behavior in the latent space, concentrating it in the first two SVD components, which leads to more effective and transferable refusal vectors for ablation attacks but also increases vulnerability to self-generated vectors.
papers.conclusion: LAT significantly alters the encoding of refusal behavior in the latent space, creating a more concentrated representation that is effective for cross-model attacks but vulnerable to self-attacks, highlighting both strengths and vulnerabilities for improving model safety.
papers.key_findings:
LAT concentrates refusal representation in the first two SVD components, explaining approximately 75% of activation differences variance.
LAT models show lower resistance to self-generated refusal ablation attacks compared to SSFT and AT.
LAT refusal vectors are more effective and transferable across different model variants.
LAT does not substantially redistribute refusal representation across network layers; layer 14 remains most effective for ablation.
LAT's training perturbations enable a more comprehensive representation of refusal behavior, but make models more vulnerable to self-attacks.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty about the exact semantic meaning of the identified directions in the latent space.
Experiments conducted exclusively on Llama-2-7B-chat, limiting generalizability to other architectures or scales.
Focus on a specific ablation technique without comprehensive evaluation of other adversarial attacks or activation steering methods.
Limited to harmful and harmless examples from the AdvBench and Alpaca datasets.
future_direction: Focus on maintaining LAT's robust representations while addressing its susceptibility to ablation attacks.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models' refusal behavior is primarily encoded in a single direction in their latent space, making it vulnerable to targeted attacks. Although Latent Adversarial Training (LAT) attempts to improve robustness by introducing noise during training, a key question remains: How does this noise-based training affect the underlying representation of refusal behavior? Understanding this encoding is crucial for evaluating LAT's effectiveness and limitations, just as the discovery of linear refusal directions revealed vulnerabilities in traditional supervised safety fine-tuning (SSFT). Through the analysis of Llama 2 7B, we examine how LAT reorganizes the refusal behavior in the model's latent space compared to SSFT and embedding space adversarial training (AT). By computing activation differences between harmful and harmless instruction pairs and applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that LAT significantly alters the refusal representation, concentrating it in the first two SVD components which explain approximately 75 percent of the activation differences variance - significantly higher than in reference models. This concentrated representation leads to more effective and transferable refusal vectors for ablation attacks: LAT models show improved robustness when attacked with vectors from reference models but become more vulnerable to self-generated vectors compared to SSFT and AT. Our findings suggest that LAT's training perturbations enable a more comprehensive representation of refusal behavior, highlighting both its potential strengths and vulnerabilities for improving model safety.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
